Strong empirical results: order-of-magnitude improvements in round-trip error across three datasets and design dimensions up to P=100
Excellent experimental methodology: fair parameter-matched baselines (INN, CFM), comprehensive evaluation metrics, and particularly insightful accuracy-conditioned diversity analysis (Figure 3)
Architecture-specific uncertainty metrics (Zero-Deviation, Self-Consistency) show consistent improvements; Zero-Deviation has no computational overhead
Exceptional reproducibility: detailed implementation details (Appendix D), hyperparameters, proofs, and dataset descriptions enabling verification
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging oracle gaps (34-57%) and INN competitiveness at high dimensions, with concrete future directions

Unclear attribution of improvements: unclear whether gains stem from fundamental algorithmic advantage vs. better numerical conditioning vs. reduced scale mismatch. Gas turbine dataset already normalized [0,1], weakening scale-robustness claims

Substantial gap to oracle performance in uncertainty quantification (34-57% for error-rejection), indicating proposed metrics, while practical, leave significant room. Metrics are somewhat natural architectural consequences rather than novel UQ concepts
Mixed high-dimensional performance: INN achieves lower forward MSE at P≥50 (Table 3), suggesting Diag-CFM doesn't universally dominate despite strong inverse advantages

Missing experimental details: OOD threshold (2-8%) appears arbitrary without sensitivity analysis; no ablation on z ∈ ℝ^(P-L) vs. ℝ^P; subtle distinction between learning-problem equivariance vs. model permutation-invariance could be clearer upfront

Limited engagement with related work: no comparison to recent physics-informed approaches like DFlow-SUR (Yang et al., 2025); unclear why ordering sensitivity wasn't identified in prior flow matching literature

strengths: Identifies and clearly demonstrates a genuine practical problem with standard CFM: ordering sensitivity in parametric inverse design (Figure 2)
Simple, intuitive solution with formal justification: Propositions 4.1-4.2 establish equivariance of target velocity distribution under permutations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three datasets (P=6 to P=100) with multiple baselines (INN, CFM) and detailed implementation details in appendices
Practical UQ metrics (Zero-Deviation) requiring no additional forward passes or ensemble training, enabling efficient uncertainty estimation
Thorough accuracy-conditioned diversity analysis (Figure 3, Appendix E) appropriately contextualizes results and avoids misleading metrics
Strong empirical results showing order-of-magnitude improvements in round-trip error on two out of three datasets
weaknesses: Core technical contribution is relatively straightforward: once ordering sensitivity is identified, symmetric augmentation follows naturally; limited conceptual novelty for top-tier venue

Overclaimed theoretical results: abstract claims 'provably invariant to coordinate permutations' and 'learning problem provably independent of coordinate ordering,' but Proposition 4.1 only establishes equivariance of target velocity distribution, not invariance of learning problem itself or model behavior

Unfair experimental comparison: Diag-CFM uses z∈ℝ^P while standard CFM uses z∈ℝ^(P-L), providing additional latent capacity; paper claims 'preserving degrees of freedom' but network capacity and information flow differ, confounding the source of improvements

Weak theoretical grounding for UQ metrics: Zero-Deviation relies on intuition that model outputs should have near-zero final coordinates, but this doesn't rigorously justify why it captures epistemic uncertainty about feasibility; Self-Consistency is essentially round-trip error checking with no novelty

Substantial gap to oracle performance: error-rejection achieves 10-27% improvement vs. 34-57% oracle, indicating UQ metrics capture something quite different from true feasibility uncertainty; at P=100, Self-Consistency OOD detection (AUC=0.51) degrades to worse-than-random performance

Scalability concerns not adequately addressed: forward MSE degrades at high dimensions (P≥50, INN outperforms Diag-CFM); raw diversity lower than baselines suggesting potential mode collapse; Self-Consistency AUC=0.51 at P=100 indicates unreliable uncertainty at scale

Experimental design concerns: (1) Surrogate models used as ground truth rather than physics simulations; (2) INN baseline uses fixed hyperparameter weights across all datasets without reported tuning; (3) OOD detection strategy (2-8% distance threshold) is somewhat arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis

Limited mechanistic understanding: paper does not explain why symmetric pairing stabilizes training beyond intuition and Figure 2; missing ablations (e.g., Diag-CFM with z∈ℝ^(P-L), standard CFM with per-ordering hyperparameter tuning)

Presentation issues: equivariance vs. invariance distinction not made sufficiently clear upfront; notation transitions (z from ℝ^(P-L) to ℝ^P) buried in discussion; overclaimed 'permutation-invariant' framing throughout

strengths: Clear problem identification: Demonstrates genuine CFM sensitivity to coordinate ordering with rigorous ablation (Figure 2, Table 4)
Elegant theoretical solution: Propositions 4.1-4.2 correctly establish equivariance properties with sound proofs; zero-anchoring strategy is principled and simple
Substantial empirical improvements: Order-of-magnitude gains in round-trip accuracy across all datasets (12× over CFM on gas turbine, 35-42× on DTLZ P=12)
Accuracy-conditioned diversity analysis: Insightful refutation of mode-collapse concerns (Figures 3, 5-6) shows Diag-CFM maintains high diversity at strict accuracy thresholds where baselines fail

Practical uncertainty metrics: Zero-Deviation is zero-overhead byproduct; both metrics consistently outperform baselines (13-31% improvement over random for select-best); systematic evaluation across three tasks
Honest evaluation and reproducibility: Acknowledges gap to oracle, provides detailed implementation details (Appendix D), reports error bars, proper ablations
Scalability demonstrated: Maintains advantages up to P=100, showing applicability to realistic high-dimensional design problems
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: Zero-anchoring is a straightforward coordinate reordering in the loss function; builds heavily on existing CFM machinery without fundamental architectural innovation

Uncertainty metrics lack theoretical justification: Zero-Deviation and Self-Consistency are empirically motivated; no principled derivation from uncertainty theory; large gap to oracle performance (34-57% for error-rejection, 81-94% for select-best) unexploited

Incomplete comparison to recent work: DFlow-SUR (2025) with physical gradient propagation not experimentally compared; limited coverage of recent generative design methods; claim about test-time optimization cost lacks direct evidence

Missing failure analysis: No discussion of when Zero-Deviation/Self-Consistency metrics fail; what dataset characteristics lead to poor uncertainty calibration; no uncertainty calibration analysis
Limited ablations on design choices: Why augment to P dimensions vs P-L? Sensitivity to 30 ODE steps? Impact of ensemble size M=5? These remain unexamined

strengths: Clear technical contribution with mathematical grounding: the zero-anchoring strategy elegantly addresses permutation sensitivity in CFM, supported by formal propositions with correct proofs

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across five diverse datasets (P=6 to 784) with substantial improvements in round-trip error and meticulous ablations (parameter ordering, surrogate robustness, ODE solvers, accuracy-conditioned diversity)
Practical uncertainty quantification metrics enabling critical deployment scenarios (abstention, OOD detection); Zero-Deviation particularly attractive as it requires no additional forward passes
Excellent reproducibility: extensive implementation details, multiple random seeds with reported standard deviations, robustness checks across different conditions, code availability promised

Thorough experimental design with fair comparisons (matched parameter counts), appropriate baselines (CFM, INN), and honest limitations discussion acknowledging gaps to oracle performance and high-dimensional forward prediction challenges
weaknesses: Incremental technical novelty: the core modification (anchoring labels to zero, pairing designs with P-dimensional noise) is straightforward; primarily an adaptation of existing CFM rather than a fundamental methodological advance

Concerning high-dimensional results undermine generality claims: standard INN achieves better forward MSE on DTLZ at P≥50 (e.g., P=100: INN 1.22×10⁻³ vs Diag-CFM 9.58×10⁻³); explanation attributed to dataset properties is insufficient and unexplored

Substantial oracle gaps in UQ metrics limit practical deployment confidence: error-rejection shows 34-57% gap between achieved and oracle performance; Self-Consistency AUC drops to 0.51 on DTLZ P=100 (near-random); investigation into causes is lacking

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Identifies genuine practical issue of CFM sensitivity to parameter ordering in inverse design (convincingly demonstrated in Figure 2)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Five diverse datasets spanning P ∈ {6-784} with consistent, substantial improvements (6.5-12× on gas turbine, 35-42× on DTLZ P=100)
Simple yet effective solution: Zero-anchoring strategy is elegant, with formal justification via Propositions 4.1-4.2 establishing permutation equivariance

Excellent supplementary materials: Thorough appendices including ablations, surrogate robustness checks, ODE solver sensitivity, accuracy-conditioned diversity analysis, and detailed UQ results strengthen confidence

Practical UQ metrics: Zero-Deviation requires no additional forward passes; both Zero-Deviation and Self-Consistency outperform ensemble baselines on select-best, error-rejection, and OOD detection tasks
Fair experimental methodology: Matched parameter counts across baselines, 5 runs per setting, appropriate metrics, and reproducibility effort through detailed implementation specifications
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Core contribution—changing [z; y] → x to [z; y] → [x; 0]—is straightforward engineering once the problem is identified, lacking deeper methodological or theoretical innovation

Overstated permutation invariance claims: Proposition 4.1 establishes distributional equivariance of target velocities, but the learned model need not be invariant (acknowledged by authors). Practical benefits appear to stem from scale matching and numerical stability rather than fundamental invariance; this distinction is not thoroughly investigated

Inconsistent high-dimensional forward prediction: On DTLZ P≥50, INN achieves better forward MSE than Diag-CFM (P=100: INN 1.22×10⁻³ vs Diag-CFM 9.58×10⁻³), contradicting universality claims. Dismissal as non-generic is unconvincing; underlying cause unexplained

Weak theoretical justification for UQ metrics: Zero-Deviation and Self-Consistency lack formal theoretical backing for why they should correlate with epistemic uncertainty. Large gap to oracle (34-57% for error-rejection). OOD AUC degrades at high dimensions (P=100: 0.73). Metrics are architecture-specific and heuristic

Limited baseline comparisons: Only CFM and INN compared; missing DFlow-SUR, alternative invertible networks, recent UQ methods (MC-dropout, Bayesian approaches). Ensemble baseline is standard but limited

Shallow mechanistic understanding: Paper demonstrates empirically that the method works but provides minimal insight into why beyond permutation equivariance. No ablation isolating the contribution of different components (zero-anchoring vs. P-dimensional augmentation vs. scale effects)
Surrogate model dependence: Gas Turbine and Unifoil evaluation depend on learned forward surrogates, adding uncertainty despite robustness checks. Reproducibility limited by proprietary simulators

Missing ablations and analysis: No justification for noise distribution choice (uniform [0,1]); no comparison of probability paths; no investigation of whether benefit is truly from permutation invariance vs. numerical conditioning; no computational cost analysis

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Figure 2 convincingly demonstrates that standard CFM exhibits strong sensitivity to parameter ordering (nearly order-of-magnitude variation), a previously under-appreciated practical issue for inverse design practitioners.

Theoretical grounding: Propositions 4.1-4.2 provide formal guarantees that Diag-CFM's target velocity is equivariant to permutations, rigorously distinguishing it from standard CFM with correct proofs.
Elegant simplicity: The zero-anchoring strategy is conceptually straightforward (pair designs with noise, labels with zero) yet achieves profound practical benefits through permutation invariance.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Five diverse datasets (P=6 to P=784), consistent 10-40× improvements in round-trip error, multiple evaluation metrics, thoughtful accuracy-conditioned diversity analysis (Figures 3, 5, 6) that provides deeper insights than raw metrics.

Statistical rigor: Results averaged over 5 runs with error bars, stable across parameter orderings and ODE solvers (Appendix E), robust to surrogate noise (Appendix D) and architecture choices (Appendix D cross-surrogate validation).

Practical uncertainty quantification: Zero-Deviation requires zero computational overhead (byproduct of generation), both metrics consistently outperform ensemble and loss-based baselines across select-best, error-rejection, and OOD detection tasks.

Reproducibility and transparency: Extensive appendices with implementation details, dataset descriptions, ablations, multiple baselines, 5 runs per experiment with error bars, and code availability mentioned.

Strong empirical results with varied problem domains: Improvements demonstrated across aerodynamics, combustor design, multi-objective optimization, photonics, and high-dimensional image statistics, indicating broad applicability.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of core technique: The zero-anchoring strategy, while effective, is a relatively straightforward modification to CFM. The conceptual insight (pair designs with noise, labels with zero) is simple, and the permutation-equivariance proof, though correct, is somewhat incremental.

Uncertainty quantification methods are heuristic rather than principled: Zero-Deviation relies on empirical observation that |s(1)[P+1:P+L]| should be small without theoretical justification. Self-Consistency's replacement of approximate with exact zeros feels ad-hoc. Gap to oracle performance (34-57% for error-rejection) indicates substantial room for improvement.

Incomplete baseline comparisons for UQ: Only ensemble variance and FM loss tested as general-purpose baselines. Missing comparisons with MC-dropout, temperature scaling, Laplace approximation, or recent Bayesian deep learning methods. Physics-based methods excluded with limited justification.

DTLZ forward prediction exception: On DTLZ at P≥50, standard INN achieves better forward MSE than Diag-CFM, weakening claims of universal superiority. While attributed to dataset-specific properties, this suggests method advantages aren't universal and deserves deeper analysis.

Surrogate-based evaluation limitations: Gas turbine and Unifoil round-trip errors evaluated using learned surrogates rather than ground truth simulators. While Appendix D provides noise robustness checks, systematic surrogate biases could persist. Unifoil surrogate trained on only fully turbulent subset.

Missing computational cost analysis: No timing comparisons versus baselines provided. ODE integration with 30 steps has computational cost but not quantified. Ensemble UQ requires training 5 models—cost mentioned but not analyzed. Comparison with optimization-based methods' computational trade-offs absent.

Limited failure mode analysis: Insufficient discussion of when Diag-CFM would underperform or when zero-anchoring could be harmful. No analysis of problem characteristics that maximize benefit. Deep domain-specificity analysis of improvements would strengthen contribution.

OOD detection methodology concerns: OOD points based on normalized nearest-neighbor distance somewhat arbitrary. 'Hard' setting (2-8% distance) is artificial; practitioners may not know when this close to boundary. Physically-grounded OOD tests (Table 14) only conducted for Unifoil, limiting generalizability.

Design diversity narrative could be clearer: Raw design diversity (Tables 1-5, 10) is often lower for Diag-CFM. Claims of 'maintaining diversity' rely on accuracy-conditioning. Paper could be more explicit that this accuracy-over-diversity trade-off is intentional and desirable.

Architectural constraints not directly integrated: Unlike DFlow-SUR and constraint-coupled methods, Diag-CFM generates designs for any target without physical feasibility checks during generation. While UQ provides post-hoc filtering, direct constraint integration during generation might improve efficiency.
